Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, right colectomy for T4N2M0 cancer 24 months ago. FDG-PET: four liver foci, 1.5-3.5 cm, no extra-hepatic. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Multiple metachronous liver involvement, surgical feasibility to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: The four hepatic lesions (1.5‑3.5 cm) are limited in number and size, suggesting that a curative‑intent hepatectomy could be feasible. However, definitive classification requires critical information that is currently missing – namely the precise segmental distribution of the lesions, their relationship to major vascular structures (portal pedicles, hepatic veins, hepatic artery), and an assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) and hepatic functional reserve. Without these data the safety of an upfront resection cannot be confirmed, therefore the case is deemed “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Obtain high‑resolution, contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) with volumetric analysis to map lesion locations, evaluate vascular involvement, and calculate FLR.  
- Perform baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR) and indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin scan to confirm adequate hepatic reserve.  
- Assuming imaging confirms that an R0 resection is technically possible with an FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % if liver is steatotic/fibrotic), initiate systemic chemotherapy as a “test of biology” and to potentially downsize lesions: preferred regimen for KRAS‑mutated disease is FOLFOX (or FOLFIRI) combined with bevacizumab for 2–3 months.  
- Re‑stage with repeat imaging after chemotherapy. If disease remains confined to the liver and FLR criteria are met, proceed to curative hepatic surgery.  
   • Preferred surgical approach: parenchymal‑sparing, anatomic or non‑anatomic resections of each lesion, aiming for negative margins while preserving maximal liver parenchyma; consider a staged approach (e.g., two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS) only if a single‑procedure resection would leave an insufficient FLR.  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion locations and guide resection.  
- Post‑operative management: resume systemic therapy (same regimen) for 3–6 months as adjuvant treatment, given high‑risk primary pathology (T4N2) and KRAS mutation.  
- Surveillance: 3‑monthly CT or MRI for the first 2 years, then 6‑monthly up to 5 years, with CEA monitoring.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Exact segmental location of each hepatic metastasis and proximity to major vessels.  
- Volumetric data: total liver volume, calculated future liver remnant, and presence of steatosis/fibrosis.  
- Quantitative liver function assessment (ICG clearance, 99mTc‑mebrofenin, or similar).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that may affect surgical risk.  
- Baseline laboratory values (bilirubin, albumin, coagulation profile, platelet count).  
- Prior systemic therapy received (neoadjuvant or adjuvant) and tolerance to chemotherapy.  
- Details of the primary tumor pathology beyond T4N2 (e.g., margin status, lymphovascular invasion).  

These data are essential to move from “Potentially resectable” to a definitive “Resectable upfront” or “Not resectable” decision and to finalize the operative plan.

Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Solitary 2.8 cm lesion confined to segment V, well within size criteria for hepatic resection.  
- No radiologic evidence of additional intra‑ or extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Patient is described as having good general condition, suggesting adequate performance status and liver functional reserve.  
- A segmentectomy of segment V would preserve sufficient future liver remnant (>30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver).  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Pre‑operative phase  
  • Initiate systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX) combined with anti‑EGFR therapy (cetuximab) for 2–3 months, given RAS wild‑type status and elevated CEA (high‑risk feature).  
  • Re‑stage with repeat liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) after chemotherapy to confirm disease stability or response.  

- Surgical phase  
  • Perform a curative‑intent anatomical segmentectomy of segment V with negative margins (R0).  
  • Intra‑operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and exclude occult additional metastases.  

- Post‑operative phase  
  • Complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative systemic therapy (i.e., continue adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery to reach the planned duration).  
  • Resume standard colorectal cancer surveillance: CEA every 3–6 months, cross‑sectional imaging of the liver every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
No essential data are missing to make a reliable resectability assessment and to formulate the above management plan.

- No extra‑hepatic disease on thoracic CT.

  • Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and chest CT at 3‑month intervals for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
  • Serial CEA measurements concurrent with imaging.  
  • Consider enrollment in a clinical trial for KRAS‑mutated colorectal liver metastases if available.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- No additional data are required to support the above recommendation; the provided information (lesion size, location, absence of extra‑hepatic disease, KRAS status, CEA level) is sufficient for a definitive management plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases and a single cerebellar metastasis at the total body CT scan. CEA 860 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Systemic disease with brain involvement, neurological priority indication.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable: the presence of multiple bilobar liver metastases and a cerebellar metastasis precludes immediate curative surgery. Resection can only be contemplated after (a) effective systemic therapy to downsize hepatic disease and (b) definitive local treatment of the brain lesion, both of which are required to achieve an R0 hepatic resection and to meet oncologic safety criteria.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Confirm performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and baseline organ function; assess cardiopulmonary reserve for major surgery.  
- Prioritize the cerebellar metastasis: if symptomatic or causing mass effect, proceed with neurosurgical resection or stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) as soon as possible; otherwise, treat with SRS.  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy with a conversion‑intention regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) while monitoring CEA and radiologic response every 8‑10 weeks.  
- Re‑stage the liver after 2‑3 months of chemotherapy: obtain contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT, calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume, and reassess number/size of lesions.  
- If imaging shows sufficient tumor shrinkage to allow an R0 resection with an adequate FLR (≥30 % in normal liver, ≥40 % after chemotherapy), plan a staged hepatic approach:  
   • Option A – two‑stage hepatectomy with portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the FLR, followed by completion hepatectomy.  
   • Option B – single‑stage major hepatectomy if disease is limited to one hemi‑liver after downsizing.  
- Address the primary colon tumor: if obstructive, bleeding, or symptomatic, perform a right hemicolectomy either before or concurrently with the liver resection (simultaneous resection considered only if hepatic surgery is limited and patient condition permits).  
- Post‑operative systemic therapy: resume or switch to maintenance chemotherapy (e.g., fluoropyrimidine ± bevacizumab) for at least 6 months, with consideration of targeted agents based on molecular profile.  
- Ongoing surveillance: CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging of chest/abdomen/pelvis every 6 months, and brain MRI annually or as clinically indicated.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- ECOG performance status and detailed comorbidities.  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Exact number, size, and distribution of hepatic lesions.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS/NRAS, BRAF, MSI/MMR status).  
- Neurological status and symptoms related to the cerebellar lesion; feasibility of surgical resection versus SRS.  
- Cardiopulmonary reserve (ejection fraction, pulmonary function tests) to tolerate major hepatectomy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with multiple bilobar liver metastases associated with a cerebellar metastasis in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (860 ng/mL). The presence of brain metastasis indicates advanced systemic dissemination and excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical strategy at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Neurological priority (mandatory)
• Immediate neurosurgical and/or radiotherapy assessment of the cerebellar metastasis is required as the first therapeutic step.
• The objective is neurological control and symptom prevention.

B. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of liver lesions
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (860 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

C. Systemic therapy after neurological stabilization
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision once neurological status is stabilized.
• The objective is global disease control.

D. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI and full-body imaging after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

E. Criteria for reconsidering liver-directed therapy (exceptional)
• Hepatobiliary surgical re-evaluation would be considered only in the rare situation of complete neurological control and major hepatic response, which remains highly unlikely.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Neurological status and resectability of the cerebellar metastasis.
B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of liver lesions.
D. Molecular profile to optimize systemic treatment.
E. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.
F. Presence or absence of additional extrahepatic disease on full staging.
G. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, T4N2 rectal tumor, six bilobar liver metastases, pulmonary micronodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 1250 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-pulmonary involvement, not resectable upfront.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – Current imaging shows six bilobar liver metastases and pulmonary micronodules, which preclude immediate curative resection. Conversion to resectability will require (a) systemic chemotherapy/targeted therapy to achieve tumor downsizing and (b) definitive assessment of the pulmonary lesions (size, number, resectability) after systemic treatment. Until these prerequisites are fulfilled, surgery cannot be performed upfront.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Initiate systemic therapy aimed at both hepatic and pulmonary disease:  
   • Preferred regimen – intensive triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOXIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) because the tumor is RAS wild‑type.  
   • Duration – 8–12 cycles, with interim imaging after 4–6 cycles to evaluate response.  

2. Simultaneously address the primary rectal tumor:  
   • Because the lesion is T4N2, give long‑course neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (50.4 Gy with concurrent capecitabine or 5‑FU) either before or interleaved with systemic chemotherapy, depending on symptom burden and multidisciplinary consensus.  

3. Restaging after systemic therapy and chemoradiation:  
   • Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase to reassess number, size, and distribution of liver lesions; calculate future liver remnant (FLR).  
   • High‑resolution chest CT (or PET‑CT) to define pulmonary nodule size, number, laterality, and resectability.  
   • Repeat CEA to gauge biochemical response.  

4. Decision point based on restaging:  
   • If liver disease is reduced to ≤4 lesions confined to one lobe or amenable to a two‑stage/ALPPS approach with adequate FLR (>30 % in normal liver, >40 % after chemotherapy), proceed with liver‑first strategy.  
   • If pulmonary nodules are ≤5, ≤3 cm each, and surgically resectable, schedule pulmonary metastasectomy either concurrently with liver surgery (if feasible) or sequentially after hepatic clearance.  
   • If hepatic disease remains extensive or pulmonary disease is diffuse/unresectable, continue systemic therapy and consider clinical trial enrollment or best‑supportive care.  

5. Surgical sequence (when criteria met):  
   • Stage 1 – Portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy of the future liver remnant.  
   • Stage 2 – Curative hepatectomy (e.g., right hepatectomy plus wedge resections or two‑stage left‑plus‑right resections) achieving R0 margins.  
   • Stage 3 – Pulmonary metastasectomy (wedge resection or segmentectomy) if lesions are resectable and patient’s pulmonary reserve is adequate.  
   • Stage 4 – Definitive rectal surgery (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection) after recovery from hepatic/pulmonary procedures, ensuring negative margins and sphincter preservation when possible.  

6. Adjuvant considerations:  
   • Post‑operative systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of FOLFOX or capecitabine) for 3–6 months based on pathology and residual disease.  
   • Consider adjuvant radiotherapy to the pelvis if margins are close or positive after rectal resection.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Exact size, number, and segmental distribution of each liver metastasis; volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
• Detailed characteristics of pulmonary micronodules (size, number, laterality, metabolic activity on PET).  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve (e.g., FEV1, DLCO).  
• Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR) and portal venous pressure.  
• Presence of symptoms from the rectal primary (bleeding, obstruction) that might dictate timing of local therapy.  
• Molecular profile beyond RAS (e.g., BRAF, MSI status) that could influence systemic regimen choice.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with six bilobar liver metastases and pulmonary micronodules in the context of a T4N2 rectal tumor and very high CEA (1250 ng/mL). The combination of extensive bilobar hepatic disease and extrahepatic pulmonary involvement reflects advanced systemic dissemination. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Thoracic surgical assessment of pulmonary nodules is required.
• Given the high CEA level (1250 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Start systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Hepatobiliary surgical re-evaluation would be considered only in the rare case of major response with significant reduction of both hepatic and pulmonary disease, allowing complete clearance of all sites.
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.

F. Pelvic management integration
• Plan rectal treatment (short-course radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy) according the MDT discussion if the primary tumor is symptomatic

G. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy according to MDT, and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

H. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• If resection, analysis ofpathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the liver metastases.
B. Characterization of pulmonary micronodules on chest CT.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and symptoms related to the primary rectum tumor : detailed pelvic MRI to plan rectal treatment.
E. Patient’s performance status for staged multimodal procedures.
F. Confirmation of absence of other extrahepatic disease on full staging.
G. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.
H. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular status of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left colon cancer, liver metastases (segments IV, V, VIII) and confirmed right iliac bone metastasis at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-osseous involvement, priority systemic management.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Classification: Not resectable  
Reasoning: The presence of a confirmed right iliac bone metastasis represents extra‑hepatic disease that is not amenable to curative resection. Current guidelines consider colorectal cancer with synchronous bone metastasis a systemic disease, for which upfront hepatic resection is not indicated. Additionally, KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR therapy but does not affect resectability; the decisive factor is the unresectable osseous lesion and the need for systemic disease control before any curative intent surgery can be contemplated.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated left‑sided colorectal cancer (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFOXIRI combined with bevacizumab).  
- Perform baseline assessment of tumor markers (CEA), liver function, and performance status.  
- After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, obtain restaging contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, pelvis and MRI or PET‑CT of the pelvis to evaluate response of both hepatic lesions (segments IV, V, VIII) and the iliac bone metastasis.  
- If hepatic disease shows significant downsizing and the bone lesion is stable or responding to systemic therapy, discuss the feasibility of local ablative approaches (e.g., stereotactic body radiotherapy or radiofrequency ablation) for liver lesions and palliative radiotherapy for the bone lesion.

Man, 65 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 970 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-peritoneal disease, goal of systemic control.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient harbors eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis, which preclude immediate curative surgery. However, conversion to resectability is possible if (a) systemic chemotherapy achieves sufficient tumor shrinkage and (b) restaging clarifies the extent of peritoneal disease and the future liver remnant (FLR). Therefore a prerequisite systemic treatment and reassessment are required before any surgical plan can be finalized.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) for 8–12 cycles, with close monitoring of CEA and tolerance.  
- Perform baseline molecular profiling (KRAS/NRAS, BRAF, MSI) to guide biologic choice and potential eligibility for targeted agents or immunotherapy.  
- After 2–3 months, obtain high‑resolution liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) and a dedicated peritoneal assessment (CT or diagnostic laparoscopy) to:  
   • Quantify response of liver lesions (size reduction, number of viable lesions).  
   • Determine the peritoneal cancer index (PCI) and assess feasibility of complete cytoreduction.  
- If imaging shows ≤5 liver metastases confined to one or two lobes with an FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % after portal vein embolization), plan a liver‑first or simultaneous approach:  
   • Consider portal vein embolization or ALPPS if FLR is marginal.  
   • Perform anatomical liver resection (e.g., right hepatectomy ± segmental resections) aiming for R0 margins.  
   • Follow with resection of the primary right colon tumor (right hemicolectomy) in the same operation if patient condition permits, otherwise schedule within 4–6 weeks.  
- If peritoneal disease is limited (PCI ≤ 10) and complete cytoreduction appears achievable, incorporate cytoreductive surgery with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) either concurrently with liver resection (if technically feasible) or as a staged procedure after hepatic surgery.  
- If response is inadequate (persistent extensive bilobar disease or high PCI), continue systemic therapy, consider liver‑directed modalities (radiofrequency ablation, stereotactic body radiotherapy) for residual lesions, and evaluate enrollment in clinical trials (e.g., immunotherapy for MSI‑high tumors).  
- Throughout treatment, maintain multidisciplinary review to adjust timing of surgery, assess liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin), and ensure patient fitness (ECOG ≤ 2, adequate cardiopulmonary reserve).

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed size, exact location, and volumetric assessment of each liver metastasis.  
- Calculated future liver remnant volume and baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance).  
- Precise peritoneal cancer index (PCI) and whether disease is resectable (e.g., involvement of small bowel mesentery, diaphragmatic surfaces).  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS/NRAS, BRAF, MSI/MMR status).  
- Baseline and trend of CEA levels beyond the single value provided.  
- Prior treatments (neoadjuvant, radiation) and any contraindications to biologic agents.  
These data are essential to confirm conversion potential, plan hepatic resection strategy, and decide on the feasibility of cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC.
